result.summary: Pausanias describes the Painted Portico (Stoa Poikile) at Athens, its statue, trophy and four famous paintings: Oenoe, Theseus and the Amazons, the fall of Troy, and Marathon. He also notes captured shields hung there.

scenes.title: Entrance and the Oenoe painting
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes the Hermes statue and a trophy over Plistarchus, then describes the painting of Athenians facing Lacedaemonians at Oenoe.

scenes.title: Amazons and the fall of Troy
scenes.summary: The paintings show Theseus fighting the Amazons and the Greeks at Ilium, with Ajax and Cassandra.

scenes.title: The battle of Marathon
scenes.summary: The Marathon painting shows the Greeks routing the barbarians into the marsh and at the Phoenician ships, with heroes and commanders.

scenes.title: Captured shields
scenes.summary: Shields taken from Scionaeans and from Lacedaemonians captured at Sphacteria hang in the portico.

alias_notes.explanation: The Painted Portico, named for its paintings.

analysis.text: The paintings join myth and recent history, placing Marathon beside Troy and the Amazons as equal Athenian glories.
The Painted Stoa served as a civic monument displaying Athenian victories and captured arms, shaping public memory.

legacy.text: The Stoa Poikile gave its name to Stoicism, since Zeno taught there.

language_notes.text: "Brazen" means made of bronze or brass; the "Market-Place" Hermes presided over trade and the agora.
"Heady fight" means a rash, intoxicating combat; Pausanias notes the painter chose the moment just before the fighting, not its height.
Themiscyra was the Amazons' home on the Thermodon; Hercules' raid there for the girdle, and their later invasion of Athens, are the earlier defeats alluded to.
Ajax (the lesser) dragged Cassandra from Athena's altar during Troy's sack, an outrage that made the Greek kings assemble to judge him.
Theseus "in the guise of putting out to sea" probably shows him rising from or going into the earth; the heroes' presence implies divine aid at Marathon.
The Polemarch was the Athenian archon in charge of the army; Callimachus held this office at Marathon.

context_notes.text: Plistarchus was a brother of Cassander, king of Macedonia, who succeeded Alexander's regent Antipater; this cavalry fight belongs to the late fourth century BC.
The Plataeans alone of the Boeotians fought beside the Athenians at Marathon in 490 BC.
Spartans surrendered on Sphacteria in 425 BC, a shock because Spartans were thought never to yield; Scione revolted from Athens in 423 BC.

literary_notes.text: The Amazons are praised as unbroken by defeat, showing Pausanias' admiration for courage and framing them as worthy opponents.
Barbarians shoving one another into the marsh gives a vivid picture of panicked rout and contrasts with the earlier equal valour.
The pitch-coated Spartan shields preserved against rust symbolize Athens' wish to keep the memory of the victory permanent.
